text: Training a neural network comes down to one question asked millions of times: if I nudge this number slightly, how much does the error change? That question has a name, the derivative, and it starts with something you can see, which is the steepness of a curve.

Draw the curve y equals x squared, and pick a point on it. Between that point and a second point a little further along, you can draw a straight line called a secant, and its slope is rise over run: how much y changed, divided by how much x changed.

Now slide the second point towards the first. The secant swings round and settles onto a line that just grazes the curve, called the tangent, and the slope it settles on is the derivative at that point. In symbols, we call the horizontal step h, and the derivative is the limit of the rise over the run as h shrinks towards zero.

There is a second way to see the same thing, and this course will lean on it often. Zoom in on the curve around the point, and keep zooming. The bend fades away and the curve looks more and more like a straight line, much as the Earth looks flat from where you stand. A smooth curve is straight when seen up close, and the derivative is the slope of that straight line.

For x squared the algebra is short. Expanding x plus h, squared, and cancelling leaves two x plus h, and as h shrinks this becomes two x. So the slope at one is two, the slope at three is six, and at zero, the bottom of the bowl, the slope is zero, because the bottom of a bowl is flat.

The derivative is itself a function. At every input it reports the local slope, so you can plot it as a second curve beneath the first. Where the original rises, the derivative is positive; where it falls, the derivative is negative; and where it turns around, at a peak or at the bottom of a valley, it crosses zero, which is exactly where a minimum can hide.

In code you rarely need the algebra to check a derivative. Take a tiny step on either side of the point, evaluate the function at both, and divide the difference by the width; this numerical derivative is how practitioners test their gradients. When a language model trains, every one of its weights receives such a slope, telling it which way to move so that its next word prediction is a little less wrong. Next, the chain rule, which tells us what happens to slopes when functions are stacked.
